solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Having taken drugs, start field event

blocks.note: someone who has taken drugs is high
to start in surprise is to jump

explanation.surface: An athlete gets doped up before starting their competition.
explanation.walkthrough: "Start" reads as the verb for beginning the event, but it is the startled jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: athletics splits into track and field, and this contest of leaping over a bar belongs to the field side.

clue.text: Pay wife to go on date

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife
a date or era is an age

explanation.surface: A man hands his wife money so she can go out on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: "Date" suggests a romantic outing, but it means a period of time, an age.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the money an employer hands over for work.

clue.text: Clouts buzzing insect

indicators.note: letters that are buzzing are whirling about, out of their order

blocks.note: taken literally as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone swats at an insect buzzing around them.
explanation.walkthrough: "Buzzing" seems to describe the insect, but it tells you to rearrange CLOUTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this swarming, crop-stripping grasshopper is one kind of insect.

clue.text: Western star with badge performing in variety

indicators.note: the letters of BADGE are put through their paces into a new arrangement

blocks.note: Tom Mix was a star of silent Western films
taken literally as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cowboy film star with a sheriff's badge appears in a variety show.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Mix was an American cowboy star of the silent era; "variety" looks like a show but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a sack of assorted things stands for any varied collection, so the phrase means a variety.

clue.text: Completed novel, a mystery

blocks.note: a completed deal is closed
a novel is a book

explanation.surface: Someone has finished writing a mystery novel.
explanation.walkthrough: "A mystery" pretends to be the genre of the novel, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A closed book is something you know nothing about, a mystery.

clue.text: Coming from Tallinn, perhaps caught short after Indian restaurant meal

blocks.note: a balti is a curry served in British Indian restaurants
caught is shortened to C, as on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: A visitor from Tallinn is taken ill after eating a curry.
explanation.walkthrough: "Caught short" means needing a toilet urgently, but here it just shortens "caught" to C.
explanation.definitionFit: Tallinn is the capital of Estonia, a Baltic state, so something from there is Baltic.

clue.text: Adult favouring wearing long apron

blocks.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
if you favour something you are for it
to long for something is to pine

explanation.surface: A grown-up who likes wearing a long apron.
explanation.walkthrough: "Long" looks like it describes the apron, but it is the verb pine.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names a sleeveless apron worn over clothes, often by children.

clue.text: Mystery in game unravelled

indicators.note: the letters of IN GAME come loose and are rewound in a new order

blocks.note: taken literally as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A puzzle within a game has finally been solved.
explanation.walkthrough: "In" is part of the letters, not a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name a puzzling thing nobody can explain.

clue.text: Definitely in a bad way on express

indicators.note: in an across clue the first part sits on, ahead of, the second

blocks.note: someone in a bad way is ill
to express something is to say it

explanation.surface: Someone is certainly in a bad way on an express train.
explanation.walkthrough: "Express" suggests a fast train, but it is the verb say.
explanation.definitionFit: "I'll say!" is an emphatic agreement, meaning definitely.

clue.text: Female collecting round Oxford, perhaps

blocks.note: a female is a she
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A woman is collecting people from around Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: "Oxford" suggests the city, but an oxford is a kind of laced shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: an oxford is a style of lace-up footwear, and 'perhaps' flags it as one kind among many.

clue.text: One poem (abridged) penned by one of the Mitfords in Cambridge?

indicators.note: an abridged poem is cut short, losing the last letter of VERSE

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a poem is a verse, cut short by one letter
Unity Mitford was one of the famous Mitford sisters

explanation.surface: One of the Mitford sisters writes a short poem while in Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mitfords were six aristocratic English sisters of the 1930s; Unity was one. The question mark shows Cambridge is only an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Cambridge is one famous seat of higher learning, and the question mark flags it as an example.

clue.text: ‘Sweet‘ clued badly by third of setters

indicators.note: CLUED done badly comes out in the wrong order
only the third letter of setters is taken

blocks.note: taken literally as the letters to rearrange
the third letter of setters

explanation.surface: A complaint that the word 'sweet' has been poorly clued by crossword setters.
explanation.walkthrough: "By" places T next to the anagram of CLUED, after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dulcet means sweet, especially of sound.

clue.text: Jazz pianist‘s number I introduced to camp

blocks.note: a count is a number, a total
taken as the letter itself
a military camp is a base

explanation.surface: A jazz pianist's tune is played to people at a camp.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after "pianist" means "is": the pianist is COUNT plus BASIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Swing-era bandleader from New Jersey played jazz piano, and 'Count' was his stage title.

clue.text: Gang leader in yarn, detective novel

indicators.note: the leader of yarn is its first letter

blocks.note: a gang is a mob
the first letter of yarn
dick is old slang for a detective

explanation.surface: A gang boss appears in a story, a detective novel.
explanation.walkthrough: "Detective novel" reads as a genre, but the detective is DICK and "novel" alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Herman Melville's 1851 whaling story is a novel.

clue.text: More than one place in the country where river’s dropped

indicators.note: R, short for river, is dropped from RURAL

blocks.note: PL is the abbreviation for place
rural means in the country; losing its R leaves URAL

explanation.surface: Several spots in the countryside where a river has fallen.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the standard abbreviation for river; the Ural is also a river, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the grammatical term for a word form denoting more than one.

clue.text: Nothing left in safe

blocks.note: with nothing left, everything is right
someone safe is unharmed and well

explanation.surface: A safe has been emptied, with nothing left inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is cryptic: if nothing is left, all is right.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: the first is cryptic, since if nothing is left then everything is right; the second is a plain synonym for unharmed.

clue.text: Soldier’s taken over facilities in homes up north

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier
facilities are toilets, loos in British slang

explanation.surface: A soldier has commandeered the toilets in northern houses.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is "has": the soldier has been taken over. Loo is British slang for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: domed snow houses built by Inuit people in the Arctic are homes up north.

clue.text: Second job in food shop during function

blocks.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a food shop
sine is a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: Someone takes a second job in a food shop while a function is on.
explanation.walkthrough: "Function" suggests a social event, but it is the mathematical sine.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names work done alongside one's main occupation.

clue.text: A particular detachment of troops

blocks.note: read as a noun: one specific point or item
a small party of soldiers given a special duty

explanation.walkthrough: "A particular" is a noun, one specific point, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: one sense is an individual point or item, the other a small party of soldiers assigned a duty.

clue.text: Secretary, calm, appears with Ecstasy tablet

blocks.note: a PA is a personal assistant, a secretary
calm water is still
surface padding: it only joins the pieces
E is slang for the drug Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A secretary seems calm after taking an Ecstasy tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ecstasy tablet" reads as one pill, but Ecstasy gives E and "tablet" alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names a small sweet or medicated lozenge, a kind of tablet.

clue.text: A plank on a yacht, maybe

blocks.note: taken as the letter itself
a plank is a flat length of sawn timber

explanation.surface: A plank of wood on a yacht.
explanation.walkthrough: "Maybe" signals a yacht is just one vessel you can be aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a yacht is one vessel you can be on, and the word means on a ship or other vehicle.

clue.text: Manage to come to party

blocks.note: two and two come to, or make, four
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone manages to turn up at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: "Manage to come" reads as one phrase, but "to come to" means add up to, MAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase means to manage with whatever is available.

clue.text: A boy enthralled by my illness

blocks.note: taken as the letter itself
a boy is a lad
taken as the letters themselves

explanation.surface: A boy is fascinated by the narrator's illness.
explanation.walkthrough: "My" looks like part of the definition, but it is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean a sickness or disease.

clue.text: On top of everything else, item for auction rejected across London, for instance

blocks.note: each item in an auction is a lot
London is an example of a capital city

explanation.surface: Worst of all, a lot was refused at auctions across London.
explanation.walkthrough: "For instance" signals that London is one example of a capital.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase introduces a final misfortune, crowning the rest, so it means on top of everything else.

clue.text: English philosopher poorly following onset of mumps

indicators.note: the onset of mumps is its first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of mumps
someone poorly is ill

explanation.surface: An English philosopher falls sick after catching mumps.
explanation.walkthrough: Poorly is British for unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: John Stuart, author of On Liberty, was a Victorian English philosopher.

clue.text: Jack, coming in low, exudes charm

blocks.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack
to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: A man called Jack walks in feeling down yet radiates charm.
explanation.walkthrough: "Low" seems to mean sad, but it is the verb for a cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: originally an African-American word for a magic amulet, it now means personal charisma.

clue.text: Ghost, one consumed by anger

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
wrath is anger

explanation.surface: A ghost that is a person eaten up by rage.
explanation.walkthrough: "One" is the Roman numeral I, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name the spirit of a dead person seen by the living.

clue.text: Rolling Stones song — lyric about diamonds, with cartoon heroine

blocks.note: a lay is a short lyric poem or song
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds
Jane was the heroine of a long-running Daily Mirror comic strip

explanation.surface: A Rolling Stones song with lyrics about diamonds and a cartoon girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane was a British newspaper comic strip famous for its heroine losing her clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the ballad appeared on the Stones' 1966 album Aftermath.
